definition: A 12-measure chord form built on I, IV, and V, usually as dominant seventh chords: I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I V. In C: C7, F7, G7. Also written twelve-bar blues.
A barre chord built from the open A (or Am) fingering, with its root on string 5.
A sharp (♯), flat (♭), or natural sign (♮) placed on a note. In sheet music it lasts until the end of the measure.
The harmony and rhythm that support a melody, such as chords in the left hand under a right-hand tune.
The mode starting on degree 6 of the major scale; identical to the natural minor scale.
A broken-chord accompaniment played lowest, highest, middle, highest, usually in eighth notes. On a C chord: C G E G.
Picking in a strict down-up-down-up pattern, with downstrokes on the beat and upstrokes between beats.
A fingerstyle guitar pattern where the thumb alternates between two bass strings on the beats. Similar in purpose to root–fifth bass on piano.
On guitar, a finger that stays on the same fret and string between two chords, making the change easier. The piano equivalent is holding a common tone.
The notes of a chord played one after another instead of together, often in order up or down.
An interval of 3 half steps spelled as a 2nd, such as F to G♯. It is the distinctive gap in the harmonic minor scale.
A triad made of two major 3rds, such as C E G♯. Written "aug" or "+".
Another word for measure: a group of beats between two bar lines.
A vertical line through the staff that marks the end of one measure and the start of the next.
On guitar, pressing several strings at once with one finger laid flat across the fret.
A guitar chord that uses a barre, usually finger 1 acting as a movable nut, so one fingering can be played at any fret.
The clef for lower notes (𝄢), also called the F clef. Its two dots surround the F3 line. Lines, bottom to top: G2 B2 D3 F3 A3; spaces: A2 C3 E3 G3.
The lowest note of a chord as played. In a slash chord such as C/E, the note after the slash.
A thick line joining the stems of eighth notes (or shorter notes) into a group.
The steady pulse of music that you tap your foot to. Also called the pulse.
On guitar, pushing or pulling a string across the fretboard to raise its pitch, usually by a half or whole step.
The raised keys on a piano, arranged in alternating groups of two and three. Each is named as a sharp or flat of a neighboring white key.
A chord whose notes are all played at the same time.
A note outside the major scale that gives the blues its sound, especially the ♭3, ♭5, and ♭7 (E♭, G♭, and B♭ in C).
A six-note scale: the minor pentatonic plus the ♭5. Degrees 1 ♭3 4 ♭5 5 ♭7. C blues: C E♭ F G♭ G B♭; A blues: A C D E♭ E G.
The hollow wooden box of an acoustic guitar that makes the strings' vibration loud enough to hear.

A repeating blues bass pattern built from chord tones plus the 6th (and often the ♭7). On guitar, often a root–fifth dyad alternating with a root–sixth dyad; on piano, a left-hand line such as C E G A B♭ A G E.
A guitar scale fingering that covers about four or five frets without shifting.
Beats per minute, the unit of tempo. 60 BPM is one beat per second.
The piece glued to the guitar body that anchors the strings at the far end.
A chord played one note at a time instead of all together.
A five-finger position with finger 1 (RH) on middle C and fingers 2–5 on D E F G; for the left hand, finger 5 on C3 and the thumb on G3.
A chord move that ends a phrase and gives a sense of rest or arrival. V→I is the strongest.

A setup step in TabBuddy that measures room noise and the delay (latency) between playing and the app hearing it, so pitch and timing checks are fair. Run it before graded practice and again after moving the device or changing instruments.
A musical conversation: one phrase (the call) is answered by another (the response).
A clamp across all guitar strings at one fret. It raises every open string by that many half steps.
One hundredth of a half step. Tuners show how many cents a note is away from its target.
Three or more different notes sounded together (or in close succession).
Moving from one chord to the next in time.
A picture of the guitar fretboard showing where to put fingers for a chord. Vertical lines are strings, horizontal lines are frets.
On guitar, the fingering a chord is played with, named after the open chord it comes from (G form, C form), regardless of the pitch it sounds at.
A sequence of chords, often written in Roman numerals, such as I–IV–V–I. Also just called a progression.
The type of a chord, set by its intervals: major, minor, diminished, augmented, and seventh-chord types such as maj7, 7, and m7.
A short name for a chord: root letter plus quality, such as C, Am, G7, or Fmaj7. A slash adds a bass note: C/E.
A note that belongs to the chord being played at that moment.
Improvising by aiming at notes of the current chord, especially on strong beats.
All twelve notes in order, each one half step apart: every key on the piano, or every fret on one guitar string.
All 12 keys arranged so each step clockwise is a perfect 5th higher: C G D A E B F♯/G♭ D♭ A♭ E♭ B♭ F. Each step clockwise adds a sharp (or removes a flat).
A symbol at the start of a staff that fixes which note each line and space stands for.
A note shared by two chords. Holding it while changing chords makes the change smooth.
Two parts or hands moving in opposite directions.
One or more measures of beats before playing starts, so you can feel the tempo. In TabBuddy it is shown visually while the app listens.
In scale fingering, bringing a finger (usually 3 or 4) over the thumb to reach the next note.
A felt pad that rests on a piano string to stop it sounding. Releasing a key lowers its damper; the sustain pedal lifts all of them.
Using only the notes of the current key or scale.
The seven chords built by stacking thirds on each note of a scale, using only notes from that scale. In a major key: I ii iii IV V vi vii°.
An interval of six half steps with the letter span of a fifth, such as B to F. One spelling of the tritone.
A diminished triad plus a diminished 7th (9 half steps above the root): stacked minor 3rds. Bdim7 = B D F A♭; Cdim7 = C E♭ G♭ B♭♭ (B♭♭ sounds as A).
A triad of two minor 3rds, such as B D F. Written "dim" or "°".
The 5th degree of a scale, or the chord built on it (V). It pulls strongly back to the tonic.
The chord built on scale degree 5 (V). It pulls strongly back to the tonic chord.
A major triad plus a minor 7th above the root, such as G7 = G B D F or A7 = A C♯ E G. It is the V7 chord of a major key and the basic chord of the blues.
The mode starting on degree 2 of the major scale: natural minor with a raised 6th (1 2 ♭3 4 5 6 ♭7). D Dorian: D E F G A B C.
A note followed by a dot, which adds half its value. Dotted half = 3 beats; dotted quarter = 1½ beats.
The first beat of a measure, usually the strongest.
Picking or strumming toward the floor.
Two different notes played together.
A barre chord built from the open E (or Em) fingering, with its root on string 6.
A note lasting half a beat in 4/4; two fit in one beat. Counted "1 & 2 &".
Two names for the same pitch, such as C♯ and D♭, or E♯ and F.
The interval of five letter names (C to G). In a triad, the note a 5th above the root.

Numbers used to write fingering. They differ by instrument. Piano: 1 thumb, 2 index, 3 middle, 4 ring, 5 little finger, the same in both hands. Guitar fretting hand: 1 index, 2 middle, 3 ring, 4 little finger (T sometimes marks the thumb); picking-hand fingers use p i m a.
Which finger plays which note. Good fingering keeps the hand relaxed and the sound connected.
Playing guitar with the thumb and fingers of the picking hand instead of a pick.
A chord with its 3rd as the lowest note, such as E G C for C major (written C/E).
The C, A, G, E, and D open-chord fingerings used as movable forms on guitar. In that order they link up the neck for any chord; also called the CAGED system.
A hand position with one finger on each of five neighboring keys, named after the note under the lowest finger.
The symbol ♭ (written b in note names like Bb3). It lowers a note by one half step: one key to the left on piano, one fret lower on guitar.
Tuned or sounding slightly too low.

A metal strip across the fretboard. Pressing a string just behind a fret shortens the vibrating length and raises the pitch. "Fret 3" also names the space just behind the third strip. Each fret is one half step.
The front of the guitar neck, where you press strings against the frets. Also called the fingerboard.
The hand that presses strings on the fretboard (the left hand for most right-handed players).
A five-finger position on G A B C D: right-hand thumb on G4, or left-hand finger 5 on G2.
A treble staff and a bass staff joined by a brace, used for piano. Middle C sits on a ledger line between them.
The 3rd and 7th of a chord. They define its quality and move smoothly from chord to chord.
A note lasting 2 beats in 4/4.
The smallest distance in Western music: one key to the very next key on the piano (black or white), or one fret on the guitar. Also called a semitone.
Short for half-diminished seventh chord: a diminished triad plus a minor 7th, such as Bm7♭5 = B D F A (also written Bø7).
A diminished triad plus a minor 7th, such as Bm7♭5 = B D F A. Written m7♭5 or ø7. It is the vii chord of a major key.
On guitar, sounding a higher note on the same string by bringing a fretting finger down hard, without picking again.
How the hand rests on the instrument. At the piano: fingers curved, playing on the pads near the tips, wrist level, thumb on its outer corner.
Playing with both hands at once. Learn each hand alone first, then combine them slowly.
Natural minor with a raised 7th, such as A B C D E F G♯ A. It makes the V chord major.
Notes sounding together, and how chords follow one another.
The top end of the guitar neck that holds the tuning pegs.
A song of praise, usually with a simple, regular melody and four-part harmony. Many older hymns are in the public domain.
Making up music on the spot within a key, scale, or chord progression.
Sounding at the intended pitch, with no audible wobble against a reference.
The distance between two notes, named by number (count letter names including both ends) and quality (major, minor, perfect, augmented, diminished).
The count of letter names from the lower note to the upper note, including both. C to E is a third (C D E).
The part of an interval name that pins down the exact size in half steps: major, minor, perfect, augmented, or diminished.
A chord arranged so a note other than the root is lowest.
The mode starting on degree 1 of the major scale; identical to the major scale.
The scale and home note (tonic) that a piece is based on, such as G major or E minor.
Sharps or flats at the start of each staff that apply to every note of those letters throughout the piece.
Easy-to-find notes on the staff used as reference points for reading, such as bass F3, middle C4, and treble G4.
The small delay between when a sound happens and when the app hears it. Calibration measures it so timing grades are fair.
Scale degree 7 when it is a half step below the tonic, as in a major or harmonic minor scale (B in C major, G♯ in A minor). It pulls up toward the tonic.
A short extra line above or below a staff for notes outside its five lines. Middle C uses one.
Smooth and connected, with no gap between notes.
Changing the sustain pedal just after each new chord: lift it as you play the chord, press it down right after. It connects chords without blurring them. Also called syncopated pedaling.
The mode starting on degree 7 of the major scale: 1 ♭2 ♭3 4 ♭5 ♭6 ♭7. B Locrian: B C D E F G A. Rarely used as a home.
A section of a song set to repeat so you can practice it.
The mode starting on degree 4 of the major scale: major with a raised 4th (1 2 3 ♯4 5 6 7). F Lydian: F G A B C D E.
A triad with a major third and a perfect fifth above the root, often described as bright. Written with the letter alone: C, G, E. Same as a major triad.
A 2nd, 3rd, 6th, or 7th of the larger size: M2 = 2, M3 = 4, M6 = 9, M7 = 11 half steps. From a major scale's tonic, these intervals reach the scale's own notes.
A five-note scale with degrees 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, such as C D E G A.
A seven-note scale with the step pattern W W H W W W H, such as C D E F G A B C.
An interval of two half steps (a whole step), such as C to D.
An interval of eleven half steps, such as C to B.
A major triad plus a major 7th, such as Cmaj7 = C E G B.
An interval of nine half steps, such as C to A.
An interval of four half steps, such as C to E (four frets on one guitar string).
A triad of a major 3rd plus a minor 3rd, such as C E G. Written as the letter alone: C.
A group of beats between two bar lines. The time signature says how many beats each measure holds. Also called a bar.
Scale degree 3, or the chord built on it (iii in major).
Natural minor with raised 6th and 7th going up (A B C D E F♯ G♯ A); in classical use it returns to natural minor going down.
The tune: a series of single notes heard as a line.
A device or app that marks a steady beat at a chosen tempo.
How TabBuddy hears you. It detects pitch and note timing only; it cannot see fingering, strings, or posture. Very low notes and heavy piano pedal are harder for it to hear.
The C nearest the middle of the piano, written C4. It sits on a ledger line between the treble and bass staves.
A triad with a minor third and a perfect fifth above the root, often described as dark. Written with m: Am, Em. Same as a minor triad.
A 2nd, 3rd, 6th, or 7th one half step smaller than major: m2 = 1, m3 = 3, m6 = 8, m7 = 10 half steps.
A five-note scale: 1 ♭3 4 5 ♭7. A minor pentatonic: A C D E G.
A scale with a lowered 3rd compared with major. The three common forms are natural, harmonic, and melodic minor.
An interval of one half step, such as E to F.
An interval of ten half steps, such as G to F.
A minor triad plus a minor 7th, such as Am7 = A C E G.
An interval of three half steps, such as A to C (three frets).
A triad of a minor 3rd plus a major 3rd, such as A C E. Written with "m": Am.
A graceful dance in 3/4 time, common in the Baroque and Classical eras.
The mode starting on degree 5 of the major scale: major with a lowered 7th (1 2 3 4 5 6 ♭7). G Mixolydian: G A B C D E F.

A scale made by starting a parent scale on a different degree, giving a new home note and a different sound. The seven modes of the major scale are Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, and Locrian.
A guitar chord fingering with no open strings, so it can slide to any fret to change the chord's root.
The seven letter names used for notes: A B C D E F G, repeating.
Describes a note with no sharp or flat (a natural note), or the sign ♮ that cancels a sharp or flat.
A seven-note scale with the step pattern W H W W H W W, such as A B C D E F G A.
A note named by a letter alone, with no sharp or flat (A B C D E F G). On the piano, the white keys.
The symbol ♮. It cancels a sharp or flat.
The long part of the guitar you hold with your fretting hand; its front face is the fretboard.
How long a note lasts, measured in beats: whole, half, quarter, eighth, and so on.
The slotted strip between the headstock and the fretboard that holds the strings at the zero-fret end.
The interval between one note and the next note with the same letter name, 12 half steps up or down. The higher note vibrates exactly twice as fast, which is why the two sound alike.
Guitar music is written one octave higher than it sounds, to keep notes on the treble staff. The treble clef sometimes has a small 8 below it to show this.
A guitar hand position where each of the four fretting fingers covers its own fret.
A guitar string played without pressing any fret. Written as fret 0.
The fixed order flats appear in key signatures: B E A D G C F.
The fixed order sharps appear in key signatures: F C G D A E B.
Spanish letters for guitar picking-hand fingers: p thumb, i index, m middle, a ring.
The minor key with the same tonic as a major key, such as C minor for C major. It has a different key signature.
Two parts or hands moving in the same direction.
The major scale a mode's notes come from. D Dorian's parent scale is C major.
A five-note scale. The major and minor pentatonic scales are the most common.
An interval of seven half steps, such as C to G or E to B.
An interval of five half steps, such as C to F.
The unison, 4th, 5th, and octave in their natural sizes: P1 = 0, P4 = 5, P5 = 7, P8 = 12 half steps.
A musical sentence: a group of notes that feels complete, often ending with a longer note or a cadence.
The mode starting on degree 3 of the major scale: natural minor with a lowered 2nd (1 ♭2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7). E Phrygian: E F G A B C D.
The hand that plucks or strums the strings (the right hand for most right-handed players).
One or more notes before the first full measure, leading into beat 1. Also called an anacrusis.
Plucking a bass note with the thumb and a higher note with a finger at the same moment.
How high or low a note sounds. Faster vibration (higher frequency) gives a higher pitch.
All notes with the same name regardless of octave, such as every C.
A practice mode where the score moves at a set tempo and you keep up.
Where the hand sits on the instrument. On guitar, named by the fret under the index finger. On piano, see five-finger position.
How you sit or stand at the instrument. At the piano: forearms about level with the keys, feet supported, back tall and relaxed.
A two-note chord of a root and a perfect fifth, with no third, written like A5. It is neither major nor minor.
TabBuddy's mode for playing a library song while the app listens, then reviewing hits, misses, and timing.
A sequence of chords. Short for chord progression.
On guitar, sounding a lower note on the same string by pulling a fretting finger off with a slight sideways pluck, without picking again.
A note lasting 1 beat in 4/4.
A 12-bar blues variation that moves to IV in measure 2 and back to I in measure 3.
The major key that shares a minor key's signature, a minor 3rd above its tonic: C major for A minor.
The minor key that shares a major key's signature, starting on the major scale's 6th degree: A minor for C major.
Movement from a tense chord or note to a stable one, such as V7 to I.
A symbol for a measured silence. Each note value has a matching rest.
Labels for chords by scale degree: uppercase for major (I, IV, V), lowercase for minor (ii, iii, vi), ° for diminished (vii°).
The note a chord is built on and named after. C is the root of C, Cm, and C7.
A chord with its root as the lowest note, such as C E G.
On guitar, the low E or A string, used to locate the lowest note (the root) of many chords and scales.
An accompaniment using only each chord's root and fifth, together or alternating.
The thin strip on the guitar bridge that the strings rest on; with the nut it sets the vibrating length.
A set of notes in order of pitch from a starting note (the tonic) to its octave.
A note's number within a scale: the tonic is 1, the next note 2, and so on up to 7.
Naming a pitch by letter and octave number, such as C4 (middle C). The number goes up by one at each C.
A chord with its 5th as the lowest note, such as G C E for C major (written C/G).
A dominant chord borrowed from another key to lead into a chord other than I. V7/V ("five of five") is the V7 of the V chord: in C major, D7 leading to G.
Another name for a half step.
A triad plus the note a 7th above the root, making four notes.
The symbol ♯ (written # in note names like F#4). It raises a note by one half step: one key to the right on piano, one fret higher on guitar.
Tuned or sounding slightly too high.
A blues rhythm played with a swung, long–short triplet feel on every beat.
Playing written music you have not practiced before.
A note lasting a quarter of a beat in 4/4; four fill one beat, counted "1 e & a".
A melodic move that jumps over one letter name, such as C to E (a 3rd). On the staff: line to line or space to space.
A chord symbol with a bass note after a slash, such as C/E (C major with E lowest).
On guitar, moving a fretting finger along the string to a new fret while the note keeps sounding.
The left piano pedal (una corda). It makes the sound softer and a little darker.
The middle pedal on many grand pianos. It sustains only the notes held down when it is pressed. On many uprights the middle pedal is a practice mute instead.
The round opening in the top of an acoustic guitar body.
Five horizontal lines and four spaces on which notes are written. Plural: staves.
The usual guitar tuning. From the thickest string to the thinnest: E A D G B E (E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4).
A melodic move to the next letter name, such as C to D (a 2nd).
Eighth notes played exactly even, as written.
Guitarists number the strings 1 to 6 from the thinnest (high E) to the thickest (low E).
A group of adjacent guitar strings used for a voicing, such as strings 3-2-1.
Brushing the pick or fingers across several guitar strings in one motion.
A repeating rhythm of downstrokes and upstrokes used to play chords on guitar.
The 4th degree of a scale, or the chord built on it (IV).
The chord built on scale degree 4 (IV).
Scale degree 6, or the chord built on it (vi in major).
Scale degree 2, or the chord built on it (ii in major).
The right piano pedal. It lifts all the dampers so notes keep ringing after the keys are released. Heavy pedal makes notes harder for the app to separate.
A rhythmic feel where pairs of eighth notes are played long–short instead of even, like the first and third notes of a triplet. Common in blues and jazz.
Accenting notes that fall between the main beats.
The speed of the beat, measured in beats per minute (BPM).
The interval of three letter names (C to E). In a triad, the note a 3rd above the root; it decides major or minor.
In scale fingering, passing the thumb under the hand to play the next note so the hand can continue up (right hand) or down (left hand).
A curved line joining two notes of the same pitch; play the first and hold through the second.
Two numbers at the start of music: the top says how many beats are in each measure, the bottom which note gets one beat. 4/4 = four quarter-note beats; 3/4 = three.
The first degree of a scale and the home note of a key; also the chord built on it (I or i).
The chord built on scale degree 1 (I in major, i in minor). It sounds like home.
To move music to a different starting note or key by shifting every note and chord by the same interval.

The clef for higher notes (𝄞), also called the G clef. Its curl circles the second line, G4. Lines, bottom to top: E4 G4 B4 D5 F5; spaces: F4 A4 C5 E5. Piano right-hand parts use it; guitar music uses it too, sounding an octave lower than written.
A three-note chord made of a root, a 3rd, and a 5th.
Three equal notes in the time normally taken by two of the same kind.
An interval of 6 half steps, such as C to F♯ or F to B. Spelled as an augmented 4th (C–F♯) or a diminished 5th (C–G♭, B–F).
A tool that listens to a note and shows whether it is flat, sharp, or in tune.
A geared knob on the headstock that tightens or loosens one string to raise or lower its pitch.
A chord or short passage at the end of a form that leads back to the beginning, such as the V7 in bar 12 of a blues.
Another spelling of 12-bar blues.
Two notes at the same pitch; the interval of 0 half steps (P1).
Picking or strumming toward the ceiling.
A short repeating chord pattern, often used to practice a scale or mode, or to wait before a melody starts.
A small, repeated wobble in pitch that makes a held note sing. On guitar it is made by the fretting finger; a piano cannot change a note's pitch once struck.
How the individual notes of one chord move to the next. Smooth voice leading keeps common tones and moves other notes by step.
The particular arrangement of a chord's notes: which octaves, which order, which note is lowest, and which notes are doubled or left out.
A practice mode where the app waits until it hears the right note or chord before moving on, with no tempo pressure.
A dance in 3/4 time with a strong first beat.
The long piano keys, named with the letters A to G. From C to C they form the C major scale.
A note lasting 4 beats, a full measure of 4/4.
Two half steps: two keys apart on the piano (skipping one) or two frets on the guitar, such as C to D or E to F♯. Also called a whole tone.
Another name for a whole step. Sometimes shortened to "tone".
